meta.headline: Every leap second on record has been an addition
meta.seoTitle: Has a leap second ever been taken away?

dek.text: Has a leap second ever been taken away? The IERS record says no: every one since 1972 has added a second to civil time.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

description.text: No leap second has ever been subtracted: the IERS table records 27 straight additions from 1972 to 2017.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

sections.name: answer
sections.heading: Every step in the record adds a second

sentences.text: The IERS table of TAI minus UTC, the record of every leap second since civil time began using them in 1972, climbs from 10 seconds to 37 seconds in 2017 without ever stepping back.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

sentences.text: Across those 27 one-second steps, every single one added a second to civil time; none subtracted one, so a leap second has never been taken away.
sentences.note: The 10 s and 37 s endpoints are the size of the gap between atomic and civil time, not a count of leap seconds; the 27 steps between them are the leap seconds. The figure block below carries all three figures with their cite.
